column2: And those two in the hut, Odysseus and the divine swineherd,
were preparing breakfast at dawn, having kindled a fire,
and had sent out the herdsmen with the herded swine.
And around Telemachus the loud-barking dogs fawned,
and did not bark as he approached. And divine Odysseus noticed
the dogs fawning, and the sound of feet came about.
At once he spoke to Eumaeus winged words:

Eumaeus, surely some comrade will come here
9	or another acquaintance, since the dogs do not bark,
10	but fawn around; and I hear the tramp of feet.
Not yet was the whole word spoken, when his dear son
stood in the doorway. And the swineherd sprang up amazed,
and from his hands fell the vessels with which he was busy,
mixing gleaming wine. And he went to meet his lord,
and kissed his head and both his fair eyes
and both his hands; and a warm tear fell from him.
As a father kindly affectionate greets his son
coming from a distant land in the tenth year,
his only, late-born one, for whom he has suffered many pains,
so then the divine swineherd to godlike Telemachus
clung and kissed him all over, as one who had escaped from death;
and lamenting he spoke winged words:

You have come, Telemachus, sweet light. I did not think
24	I should see you again, when you went in the ship to Pylos.
25	But come now go in, dear child, that I may take pleasure
26	in my heart looking at you, newly come from elsewhere into the house.
27	For you do not often come to the farm and the herdsmen,
28	but stay in the town; for so it has pleased your heart,
29	to look upon the destructive throng of the suitors.
And discreet Telemachus answered him:

So it shall be, father; for your sake I come here,
32	to see you with my eyes and hear your word,
33	whether my mother still remains in the halls, or whether some
34	other man has already married her, and Odysseus's bed
35	perhaps lies, for want of sleepers, with foul cobwebs.
And again the swineherd, leader of men, said to him:

Indeed she remains with an enduring heart
38	in your halls; and miserable for her always
39	the nights and days wear away as she sheds tears.
So speaking he took from him the bronze spear;
and he went inside and crossed the stone threshold.
As he approached, his father Odysseus gave up his seat to him;
but Telemachus from the other side held him back and said:

Sit, stranger; and we shall find a seat elsewhere
45	in our farmstead; and here is a man who will set it.
So he spoke, and he went back and sat down; and for him the swineherd
spread green brushwood below and a fleece above;
there then the dear son of Odysseus sat down.
And the swineherd set before them platters of roast meat,
which they had left over from the day before when they ate,
and quickly heaped up bread in baskets,
and mixed honey-sweet wine in a wooden bowl;
and he himself sat opposite divine Odysseus.
And they put out their hands to the food ready laid before them.
But when they had put away desire for drink and food,
then Telemachus spoke to the divine swineherd:

Father, from where has this stranger come to you? How did sailors
58	bring him to Ithaca? Who did they claim to be?
59	For I do not think he came here on foot.
And answering him you said, swineherd Eumaeus:

Well then, child, I shall tell you all the truth.
62	He claims descent from broad Crete,
63	and says he has wandered through many cities of mortals,
64	roaming; for so a god has spun it for him.
65	Now, having run away from a ship of Thesprotian men,
66	he has come to my farmstead, and I shall put him in your hands;
67	do as you wish; he claims to be your suppliant.
And discreet Telemachus answered him:

Eumaeus, you have said a very heart-grieving word;
70	for how shall I receive the stranger in my house?
71	I myself am young and do not yet trust my hands
72	to defend a man, when someone attacks first;
73	and my mother's heart is divided in her breast and ponders
74	whether to stay here with me and keep the house,
75	respecting her husband's bed and the talk of the people,
76	or whether to follow at once whoever is best of the Achaeans
77	and woos her in the halls and offers most.
78	But as for the stranger, since he has come to your house,
79	I shall clothe him in a cloak and tunic, fair garments,
80	and give him a two-edged sword and sandals for his feet,
81	and send him where his heart and spirit bid.
82	Or if you wish, keep and tend him in the farmstead;
83	and I shall send clothes here and all the bread
84	to eat, so that he does not wear you out and your comrades.
85	But I would not allow him to go there among the suitors;
86	for they have exceedingly reckless insolence;
87	lest they mock him, and it be a dreadful grief to me.
88	And it is hard for one man, though mighty, to accomplish anything
89	among many, since they are far stronger.
And again much-enduring divine Odysseus said to him:

Friend, since indeed it is right for me to answer too,
92	truly my dear heart is torn as I hear
93	what reckless things you say the suitors devise
94	in your halls, against your will, though you are such a man.
95	Tell me, whether you submit willingly, or the people
96	hate you throughout the land, following the voice of a god,
97	or you find fault with your brothers, in whom a man
98	trusts as they fight, even if a great strife arises.
99	Would that I were so young with this same spirit,
100	either the son of blameless Odysseus or himself;
102	at once then a stranger might cut off my head,
103	if I did not become an evil to all of them,
104	coming to the hall of Odysseus son of Laertes.
105	And if they overpowered me by their numbers, being alone,
106	I would rather be slain in my own halls
107	and die, than always see these shameful deeds,
108	strangers ill-treated and women servants
109	dragged about shamefully through the fair house,
110	and wine drawn off, and men eating bread
111	idly, without end, in a work that is never finished.
And discreet Telemachus answered him:

Well then, stranger, I shall tell you very exactly.
114	Neither is the whole people hostile to me and angry,
115	nor do I find fault with brothers, in whom a man
116	trusts as they fight, even if a great strife arises.
117	For thus the son of Kronos has made our line single:
118	Arceisius begot only Laertes as son,
119	and the father begot only Odysseus; and Odysseus
120	begot only me in the halls and left me, and had no joy of me.
121	Therefore now very countless enemies are in the house.
122	For as many as are the best rulers on the islands,
123	in Dulichium and Same and wooded Zacynthus,
124	and as many as lord it over rugged Ithaca,
125	so many woo my mother, and wear down the house.
126	And she neither refuses the hateful marriage, nor can she
127	bring it to an end; and they waste away by eating
128	my house; soon they will break me too to pieces.
129	But these things lie on the knees of the gods.
130	Father, you go quickly, and tell prudent Penelope
131	that I am safe and have come from Pylos.
132	And I shall stay here, and you come back here,
133	having told her alone; and let none of the other Achaeans
134	learn of it; for many devise evils against me.
And answering him you said, swineherd Eumaeus:

I understand, I take heed; you bid one who understands.
137	But come, tell me this and recount it truly,
138	whether on the same road I should bring the news also to Laertes,
139	ill-fated man, who for a time, grieving greatly for Odysseus,
140	would oversee the work, and with the servants in the house
141	drink and sit, when his heart in his breast bade him;
142	but now, since you went in the ship to Pylos,
143	they say he has not eaten or drunk as before,
144	nor looked on the work, but with groaning and lament
145	sits mourning, and the flesh wastes round his bones.
And discreet Telemachus answered him:

More grievous, but nevertheless we shall let him be, though grieved;
148	for if all things were somehow the choice of mortals,
149	first of all we should choose the day of my father's return.
150	But you, having told her, come back, and do not roam
151	over the fields after him; but tell my mother
152	to send the housekeeper maidservant as quickly as possible
153	in secret; for she could bring the news to the old man.
He spoke, and urged on the swineherd; and he took his sandals in his hands,
and binding them under his feet went to the city. And Athena did not
fail to notice Eumaeus the swineherd going from the farmstead,
but she came near; and she took the form of a woman
fair and tall and skilled in splendid works.
She stood at the door of the hut, appearing to Odysseus;
and Telemachus did not see her face to face nor notice,
for the gods do not appear plainly to all,
but Odysseus and the dogs saw her, and did not bark,
but with whining fled to the other side of the farmstead.
And she nodded with her brows; and divine Odysseus noticed,
and went out of the hall beside the great wall of the courtyard,
and stood before her; and Athena spoke to him:

Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus of many devices,
168	now speak the word to your son, and do not hide it,
169	so that, having arranged death and doom for the suitors,
170	you two may go to the famous city; and I myself
171	shall be eager to fight beside you, far from you no longer.
She spoke, and Athena touched him with her golden wand.
First she put on him about his breast a well-washed robe
and tunic, and increased his stature and youth.
Again he became dark-skinned, and his jaws were filled out,
and dark-blue grew the beard about his chin.
She, having so done, went away; and Odysseus
went into the hut; and his dear son was amazed at him,
and in fear turned his eyes aside, lest it be a god,
and he spoke to him winged words:

Stranger, you appear different to me now than before,
182	you have other clothes, and your skin is no longer the same.
183	Surely you are some god, of those who hold the broad heaven;
184	but be gracious, that we may give you pleasing sacrifices
185	and golden gifts, well wrought; and spare us.
And then much-enduring divine Odysseus answered him:

I am no god; why do you liken me to the immortals?
188	But I am your father, for whose sake you groan
189	and suffer many pains, submitting to the violence of men.
So speaking he kissed his son, and from his cheeks
let a tear fall to the ground; before, he had always held it back unceasingly.
But Telemachus, for he did not yet believe that this was his father,
again answered him and spoke with words:

You are not Odysseus, my father, but a spirit
195	enchants me, so that I may groan still more, lamenting.
196	For no mortal man could contrive this
197	by his own mind, unless a god himself came
198	and easily, if he wished, made him young or old.
199	For just now you were old and wore shameful clothes;
200	but now you are like the gods who hold the broad heaven.
And answering him wise Odysseus said:

Telemachus, it does not become you, when your dear father is within,
203	to wonder at him overmuch or be amazed;
204	for no other Odysseus will ever come here,
205	but here am I, such as I am, having suffered evils, and wandered much,
206	come in the twentieth year to my fatherland.
207	But this is the work of Athena the driver of spoil,
208	who made me such as she wishes, for she can,
209	at one time like a beggar, at another again
210	like a young man with fair clothes on his skin.
211	For it is easy for the gods who hold the broad heaven
212	both to exalt a mortal man and to abase him.
So speaking he sat down, and Telemachus
threw himself about his noble father and wept, shedding tears,
and in both of them a longing for lamentation rose;
and they cried shrilly, more thickly than birds,
sea-eagles or crook-taloned vultures, whose young
farmers have taken before they were fledged;
so they shed piteous tears from beneath their brows.
And the light of the sun would have set on them as they wept,
if Telemachus had not suddenly said to his father:

In what ship now, dear father, did sailors
223	bring you to Ithaca? Who did they claim to be?
224	For I do not think you came here on foot.
And again much-enduring divine Odysseus said to him:

Well then, child, I shall tell you the truth.
227	The Phaeacians brought me, famed for ships, who also send on
228	other men, whoever comes to them;
229	and bringing me asleep in a swift ship over the sea
230	they set me down in Ithaca, and gave me splendid gifts,
231	bronze and gold in plenty and woven clothing.
232	These lie in caves by the gods' will;
233	and now I have come here at the prompting of Athena,
234	that we may plan about the slaughter of our enemies.
235	But come, count the suitors and tell me,
236	that I may know how many and who the men are;
237	and pondering in my blameless heart
238	I shall consider whether we two can face them
239	alone without others, or whether we must seek others.
And discreet Telemachus answered him:

O father, always I heard of your great fame,
242	that you were a spearman with your hands and wise in counsel;
243	but you have said something too great; awe holds me; it could not be
244	that two men fight against many and mighty ones.
245	Of the suitors there are not exactly ten, nor only two tens,
246	but far more; and soon you will know the number here.
247	From Dulichium fifty-two
248	chosen young men, and six servants follow;
249	from Same there are twenty-four men,
250	from Zacynthus there are twenty young men of the Achaeans,
251	from Ithaca itself twelve, all the best,
252	and with them is Medon the herald and the divine singer
253	and two attendants, skilled in carving.
254	If we meet all of these within the house,
255	see that you do not pay for their violence bitterly and terribly on coming.
256	But you, if you can think of some defender,
257	consider, someone who would defend us two with ready heart.
And again much-enduring divine Odysseus said to him:
And discreet Telemachus answered him:

Good defenders are these two, whom you mention,
264	though seated high in the clouds; who rule also over others,
265	both men and immortal gods.
And again much-enduring divine Odysseus said to him:

Those two will not be apart for long
268	from the strong fray, when between the suitors and us
269	in my halls the might of Ares is decided.
270	But you now go at dawn
271	home, and mingle with the overbearing suitors;
272	and the swineherd will lead me to the city later,
273	like a wretched old beggar.
274	And if they dishonour me in the house, let your dear heart
275	endure in your breast while I am ill-treated,
276	even if they drag me by the feet through the house to the door
277	or pelt me with missiles; you, looking on, hold back.
278	But bid them indeed to stop their folly,
279	speaking to them with honeyed words; but they will not
280	obey you; for the day of fate stands by them.
281	And another thing I shall tell you, and lay it in your mind:
282	when the very wise Athena puts it in my mind,
283	I shall nod to you with my head, and you then, noticing it,
284	carry all the arms of war that lie in the hall
285	and lay them away in the recess of the high chamber,
286	every one; and the suitors with soft words
287	put off, when they ask you out of longing:
288	'I put them away out of the smoke, since they are no longer like
289	what Odysseus once left when he went to Troy,
290	but are defaced, as far as the breath of fire reached.'
291	And besides this the son of Kronos put a greater thing in my mind,
292	lest somehow, made drunk with wine, raising a quarrel among you,
293	you wound one another and bring shame on the feast
294	and the wooing; for iron itself draws a man on.
295	But leave for us two alone two swords and two spears
296	and two ox-hide shields to take in our hands,
297	so that rushing on we may seize them; and the others
298	Pallas Athena will beguile, and counselling Zeus.
299	And another thing I shall tell you, and lay it in your mind:
300	if you are truly mine and of our blood,
301	let no one hear that Odysseus is within,
302	neither let Laertes know it, nor the swineherd,
303	nor any of the household, nor Penelope herself,
304	but you and I alone shall learn the women's inclination;
305	and we should also test some of the men servants,
306	both who honours us two and fears us in heart,
307	and who does not care, and dishonours you, such as you are.
And answering him his glorious son said:

O father, my spirit, I think, you will know
310	later too; for no slackness of mind holds me;
311	but I do not think this will be of profit
312	to us both; and I bid you consider.
313	For you will long go about idly testing each,
314	going from farm to farm; and they in the halls at ease
315	devour the wealth insolently, and there is no sparing.
316	But I bid you learn about the women,
317	who dishonour you and who are guiltless;
318	but of the men I would not wish that we
319	test them in the farmsteads, but that this be done later,
320	if you truly know some sign from aegis-bearing Zeus.
So they spoke such things to one another;
and meanwhile the well-built ship was being brought down to Ithaca,
which carried Telemachus from Pylos and all his comrades.
And when they came inside the deep harbour,
they drew the black ship up onto the land,
and the high-spirited attendants took away their gear,
and at once carried the very beautiful gifts to Clytius's house.
And they sent a herald to the house of Odysseus
to tell the news to prudent Penelope,
that Telemachus was in the country, and had bidden the ship
sail to the city, lest the mighty queen, afraid in her heart,
shed tender tears.
And the herald and the divine swineherd met
on the same errand, to tell the woman.
But when they came to the house of the divine king,
the herald spoke among the maidservants in the midst:
Already, queen, your dear son has come.
And to Penelope the swineherd, standing near, said
all that her dear son had bidden him tell.
And when he had delivered the whole message,
he went to the swine, and left the courts and the hall.
And the suitors were grieved and downcast in their hearts,
and went out of the hall beside the great wall of the courtyard,
and sat down there before the doors.
And among them Eurymachus, son of Polybus, began to speak:

Friends, a great deed has been boldly accomplished
347	by Telemachus, this journey; we said it would not be accomplished.
348	But come, let us launch a black ship, the best,
349	and gather rowers, sailors, who most quickly
350	may tell those men to come home swiftly.
Not yet was it all said, when Amphinomus saw the ship,
turning from his place, inside the deep harbour,
and men furling the sails and holding oars in their hands.
And laughing sweetly he spoke among his comrades:

Let us send no more message; for these are inside.
356	Either some god told them this, or they themselves saw
357	the ship passing by, and could not catch it.
So he spoke, and they stood up and went to the sea-shore,
and at once drew the black ship up onto the land,
and the high-spirited attendants took away their gear.
And they themselves went in a body to the assembly, and no one else
did they allow to sit with them, neither of the young nor the old.
And among them Antinous spoke, the son of Eupeithes:

Alas, how the gods have freed this man from evil.
365	By day scouts sat on the windy heights
366	continually one after another; and at the going down of the sun
367	never did we spend the night on land, but on the sea
368	sailing in a swift ship we waited for divine Dawn,
369	lying in wait for Telemachus, to catch and destroy
370	him; but meanwhile a god led him home.
371	And let us here plan a grievous destruction
372	for Telemachus, and let him not escape us; for I do not think
373	that while he lives these works of ours will be accomplished.
374	For he himself is knowing in counsel and in wit,
375	and the people no longer wholly show favour to us.
376	But come, before he calls the Achaeans together
377	to the assembly—for I think he will not let it go,
378	but will be wrathful, and standing up will say among all
379	that we planned sheer murder for him and did not catch him;
380	and they will not approve, hearing of evil deeds;
381	lest they do us some harm and drive us out
382	of our land, and we come to the land of others—
383	but let us anticipate and take him in the country away from the city
384	or on the road; and let us keep his livelihood and goods ourselves,
385	dividing them rightly among us, and the house again
386	let us give to his mother to have and to whoever marries her.
387	But if this word displeases you, and you wish
388	him to live and to have all his father's property,
389	then let us not go on eating his goods to our heart's content
390	gathering here, but let each from his own hall
391	woo her with bridal gifts, seeking; and she then
392	may marry whoever gives most and comes as destined.
So he spoke, and they all became hushed in silence.
And among them Amphinomus spoke and said,
the glorious son of Nisus, son of lord Aretes,
who from Dulichium, rich in grain and grass,
led the suitors, and especially pleased Penelope
with his words; for he was of good mind;
and he, with kind intent, spoke and said among them:
So spoke Amphinomus, and his word pleased them.
At once then they stood up and went to the house of Odysseus,
and coming they sat down on polished chairs.
And prudent Penelope thought of another thing,
to appear to the suitors who had overbearing insolence.
For she had learned of the destruction of her son in the halls;
for the herald Medon told her, who had heard their counsels.
She went to the hall with her attendant women.
And when bright among women came to the suitors,
she stood by the pillar of the close-built roof,
holding her shining veil before her cheeks,
and rebuked Antinous and spoke a word and addressed him:

Antinous, full of insolence, deviser of evil, and yet they say
419	that in the land of Ithaca among your age-mates you are the best
420	in counsel and speech; but you are not such a one.
421	Madman, why do you stitch death and fate for Telemachus,
422	and take no heed of suppliants, for whom Zeus
423	is witness? And it is not right to stitch evil against one another.
424	Do you not know when your father came here fleeing,
425	fearing the people? For they were exceedingly angry,
426	because, following Taphian pirates, he had
427	harmed the Thesprotians; and they were friendly to us;
428	him they wished to destroy and tear out his dear heart
429	and devour his great substance to their heart's content;
430	but Odysseus held them back and restrained them in their eagerness.
431	His house you now eat, dishonoured, and woo his wife
432	and would kill his child, and greatly grieve me;
433	but I bid you stop and bid the others.
And Eurymachus, son of Polybus, answered her:

Daughter of Icarius, prudent Penelope,
436	take heart; let not these things trouble your mind.
437	There is not that man, nor will be, nor will be born,
438	who will lay hands on Telemachus your son,
439	while I live and see upon the earth.
440	For so I shall say, and it will indeed be fulfilled:
441	at once his dark blood shall run about our spear,
442	since Odysseus the sacker of cities also
443	often, setting me on his knees, put roast meat
444	in my hands and held to me red wine.
445	Therefore Telemachus is by far the dearest of all
446	men to me, and I bid him not at all fear death
447	from the suitors; but from the gods it is not possible to escape.
So he spoke encouraging, but himself was preparing destruction for him.
She went up to the shining upper chamber
and then wept for Odysseus, her dear husband, until
grey-eyed Athena cast sweet sleep on her eyelids.
And in the evening the divine swineherd came
to Odysseus and his son; and they were preparing supper,
standing, having sacrificed a yearling pig. And Athena,
standing near, to Odysseus son of Laertes
striking him with her wand made him an old man again,
and put wretched clothes about his skin, lest the swineherd
know him, seeing him face to face, and go and tell
prudent Penelope and not keep it in his mind.
And Telemachus spoke first to him:

You have come, divine Eumaeus. What is the news in the city?
462	Are the proud suitors already inside
463	from the ambush, or do they still watch for me as I go home?
And answering him you said, swineherd Eumaeus:

I did not care to ask and inquire about this
466	as I went down to the city; my heart bade me, as quickly as possible,
467	having told the message, to come back here.
468	And a swift messenger from your comrades met me,
469	a herald, who first told your mother the word.
470	And another thing I know; for I saw it with my eyes.
471	Already above the city, where the hill of Hermes is,
472	I was going, when I saw a swift ship coming down
473	into our harbour; and there were many men in it,
474	and it was loaded with shields and double-edged spears;
475	and I thought they were those men, but I do not know.
So he spoke, and the sacred might of Telemachus smiled,
looking at his father with his eyes, and avoided the swineherd.
And when they had ceased from their work and prepared the meal,
they feasted, nor did their hearts lack the equal feast.
But when they had put away desire for drink and food,
they thought of bed and took the gift of sleep.
